title: Beyond the fear of death
hook: praising the One who ends all things loosens the fear of our own ending

segments.voice: Yesterday, present in every land, and your line, in every land. Did you wish a faraway place well? Today, a gentle day about the hardest subject there is. Day three hundred fifty-four.
screen: `PRESENT IN EVERY LAND — IN EVERY LAND.`

segments.voice: There are plenty of ways of not thinking about it. We change the subject. We say passed away instead of died. We get through a funeral and go straight back to email. And then, at three in the morning, or in a hospital corridor, or on the anniversary of someone's going, the thought comes anyway: one day, me too. Traditions answer that three a.m. thought in different ways. Jaap Sahib answers it in a surprising way, not by talking about death less, but by naming the One who holds it. Today: beyond the fear of death.
screen: `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `THE THREE A.M. THOUGHT.` → `JAAP NAMES WHO HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: All through Jaap, the One is praised as the ender of all things. Sarab kaal. And in one bhujang prayat line, namo kaal kaale: salutation to the death of death, the One who is the end even of endings. It might seem a grim thing to say every morning. But follow the logic. If death were a stranger, an enemy who could sneak up from outside, then fear would make sense. Jaap says it isn't. Death isn't a rival power. It's in the One's hand, the same hand Jaap has called merciful, the house of compassion, the sustainer of all. In Jaap's picture, an ending isn't decided by a stranger. It's held by the One saluted every dawn. Sikh scripture goes further, and some of its voices meet death almost gladly. Bhagat Kabir, whose words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that the death the whole world fears fills his mind with joy, because only through dying comes perfect, supreme bliss. Sikh teaching speaks of the soul returning to its source, like a drop to the ocean. That shapes how Sikhs mourn. At a Sikh funeral, people recite Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas. The Sikh code of conduct asks mourners not to wail or beat their chests, but to recite gurbani and remember Waheguru. Grief is real, and tears are human; no one is asked to pretend. But the hymns are recited anyway, because, as Sikhs see it, the one who has gone has gone home. Death is in his hand. In Jaap's picture, so is everyone death touches.
screen: `NAMO KAAL KAALE: DEATH OF DEATH.` · `NOT A STRANGER: IN THE ONE'S HAND.` · `KABIR: THE DEATH THE WORLD FEARS.` · `AT A FUNERAL, SOHILA AND ARDAS.` · then, large: `DEATH IS IN HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit one minute with calm. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow down. Notice that every out-breath is a small letting go, and every in-breath comes back without you asking. If someone you love has died, you can hold them gently in mind; if that's too heavy today, simply rest. Let your hands lie open in your lap, as if resting in larger hands. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Beyond the fear of death. In Jaap, death is not a stranger but in the hand of the One praised as merciful, so fear can loosen.
screen: `BEYOND THE FEAR OF DEATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: death is in his hand. Today, if the three a.m. thought comes, let these words sit beside it, and then do one loving thing while there's time. Day three hundred fifty-four.

fork.setup: Bhagat Kabir thinks about the death that the whole world fears. what does he say it does to his mind?
options: fills it with joy, because through it comes supreme bliss.
makes him stop thinking about it.
fork.reveal: in his salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says the death the world fears brings him joy: only through it comes perfect, supreme bliss.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kaal, time and death; Jaap salutes the One as kaal kaale, the death of death.

trapdoor: what you thought: praising the One who ends all things sounds frightening.
what it means: death isn't a stranger; it's held by the One praised as merciful, so the fear can loosen.
what a scholar hears: 'namo kaal kaale' in the bhujang prayat; Kabir's salok at Ang 1365; the Rehat Maryada's funeral guidance discourages wailing.
